fr:mainmatter.html:p: The keys and values of every token seen so far, held in memory across decoding steps so that each is projected once rather than once per step. Attention at step t needs k_j and v_j for every j \le t, and each of those is a function of token j and the weights alone — nothing about it depends on t. So it is computable once and never again, and the only real question is whether you will spend memory to avoid recomputing it.

The cost of not spending it is quadratic, which is easy to miss because per step it looks merely linear: admitting token t means rebuilding t+1 key–value pairs, so a sequence of S tokens costs \sum _{t=1}^{S} t = S(S+1)/2 projections rather than S. The query is the asymmetry that makes the trade available at all — only the newest position needs one, so q_t is a single row either way, and decoding is a matrix–vector product against a K and V that grow by one row a step.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Notation. Following the scaling book: S is the KV sequence length, K the number of key/value heads, H the head dimension, L the layers, B the batch. The clash between K as a matrix and K as a head count is unfortunate and universal.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: What the cache costs is memory, and the shape of that cost is the reason it governs inference planning. Each token contributes a key and a value in every layer, so a batch holds

which is linear in the sequence length and — unlike the weights — per sequence, so it cannot be amortised over the batch. Context length and batch size are therefore drawn from the same High bandwidth memory budget, and past a certain context the cache dominates residency outright, which is Processing in Memory for ML's framing of the memory wall.

It also decides what decoding is bound by. At step t the model streams the entire cache through the Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) to do O(S) multiply-accumulates against a single query row, so the Arithmetic intensity is roughly one FLOP per byte read — far below the ridge point of any accelerator, and flat in S. Decoding is bandwidth-bound, and the cache is what it is bound by.

Every fix for that attacks a factor in the expression above rather than the idea of caching. MQA sets K = 1 and shares one key/value head across all query heads; Group Query Attention sets it to a group count and interpolates; Sliding Window Attention bounds S instead by refusing to attend past a window. The FLOPs are unchanged in all three — what changes is how many bytes have to move to supply them.

fr:title.text: The KV cache scales with K, and is per-sequence

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The KV cache scales with K, and is per-sequence

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How large is a KV-cache, and which dimension actually drives it?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The cache has shape [2, S, L, K, H] per sequence — the leading 2 is keys and values — so in int8 it is 2SLKH bytes.
Worked: S = 8\mathrm {k}, L = 64, KH = D = 8192 gives 2 \cdot 8192 \cdot 64 \cdot 8192 \approx 8 GiB for a single sequence.
Two things in that expression decide inference planning. It scales with K, the number of key/value heads, and not with the N query heads — which is the whole argument for Group Query Attention and MQA at K \ll N. And it is per sequence, so unlike the weights it cannot be amortised over the batch: it competes with batch size for the same High bandwidth memory budget, and generation is bandwidth-bound on streaming it.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Dot-product attention costs 12BT^2NH FLOPs in training. At what sequence length does it start to dominate the matmul FLOPs, and why that number?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Past T > 8D. With the usual proportions F = 4D, D = NH, N = K, the ratio of attention to everything else is
\frac {12BT^2NH}{18BTDF + 24BTDNH} = \frac {12BT^2D}{72BTD^2 + 24BTD^2} = \frac {T}{8D}
What that means in practice. At D \approx 8\mathrm {k} attention only takes over past roughly 64k tokens; Gemma-27B, with D = 4608, crosses at about 37k. Larger models push the crossover further out, so the quadratic term is not what stops large models training on long context — the KV-cache at inference is a much earlier wall.
The 12BT^2NH is two matmuls, QK^{\top } and SV, each 6BTSNH and each batched over B and the head axis.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: GQA saves cache, not projection FLOPs

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Per layer, what do the QKVO projections cost in parameters and training FLOPs under Group Query Attention with N query heads, K key/value heads, and head dimension H?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Parameters: 2D(N+K)H, from W_Q[D,N,H] and W_O[N,H,D] at DNH each, plus W_K, W_V[D,K,H] at DKH each.
Training FLOPs: 12BTD(N+K)H — each projection is 6BTD \cdot (\text {heads}) \cdot H.
The variants are one knob. K = N is plain multi-head attention; K = 1 is MQA; 1 < K < N with K \mid N is grouped-query, with group size G = N/K.
Read the formula for what shrinking K actually buys. It touches only the K term, so the projection cost falls from 2N to N + K — at most a factor of two, and usually far less. That is not why anyone uses GQA. The payoff is the KV-cache, which scales with K alone and is the binding constraint at generation time.

fr:title.text: POTW: Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: POTW: Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Notes on the paper Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need.

For,
b batch dimension,
n sequence length,
d hidden dimension,
h number of heads. The total FLOPS for attention are roughly bnd^2. This comes from
3nd^2 FLOPS to compute Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V.
Need to do this b times for each input in batch. and the total memory accesses are roughly \underbrace {bnd}_{X} + \underbrace {bhn^2}_{\text {softmax}} + \underbrace {d^2}_{\text {projection}}. This gives high arithmetic intensity O\left (\left (\frac {h}{d} + \frac {1}{bn}\right )^{-1}\right )

However, if we do incremental inference then we must multiply our total number of memory accesses by n i.e. bn^2d + nd^2. This gives arithmetic intensity O\left (\left (\frac {n}{d} + \frac {1}{b}\right )^{-1}\right ), which requires large batch and short sequence length.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. I believe we just ignore the softmax memory contribution in the inference case because it does not scale with n anymore as we are computing the logits just for the next token. Therefore, it becomes a \frac {d}{h} term, which we can safely ignore?
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The key is that the \frac {n}{d} term comes from the bn^2d term, where we are loading h (b \times n \times d / h) K and V matrices n times. Thus, we can improve the \frac {n}{d} term by a factor of h by simply not using a different K and V matrix for each head. This is the entire idea behind MQA.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Similar to the KV-cache, we still can use h Q matrices because we do not need to load n of them into memory because only the last one matters for inference.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Group query attention is the same idea as MQA but instead of using one K and V for every head, they use a group of them. Where obviously the number of groups needs to be less than the number of heads.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A core component of the TPU architecture responsible for performing matrix multiplication via a weight stationary Systolic array.

Tiling the matrix to load from HBM to VMEM.
Compiler tiles from VMEM to 128 \times 128 tiles to load into the MXU.

fr:title.text: Why the MXU pads everything to 128

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why the MXU pads everything to 128

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is the native op of one Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU), and why does that force padding to 128?

html:div.html:details:
Answer One bf16[8,128] @ bf16[128,128] -> f32[8,128] every 8 cycles, on a 128 \times 128 systolic array — 256 \times 256 on v6e/Trillium.
The array's side length is fixed in hardware, so any matrix axis shorter than 128 (256 on v6e) is padded up to it, and the FLOPs spent on the padding are simply wasted. With 2–4 MXUs per core, tiling dimensions want to exceed 128 \times the MXU count.
Scale: roughly 5e13 bf16 FLOPs/s per MXU at 1.5 GHz, so about 2e14 per v5e chip. int8 runs ~2\times faster, int4 ~4\times .
